root: ^Mial was down to his last health potion.
^His hands trembled. One more feral caveman awaited him—a crude, violent creature.
^After countless failed dodge rolls that had dented both his pride and his helmet, Mial finally admitted a harsh truth: he was terrible at evading in heavy armor.
^"A real adventurer," he muttered, "would’ve studied this beast’s wild swings. If only I could read his patterns... maybe I could parry him, and then strike!"
^Climbing a rock, Mial watched the beast swing away in confusion. "I'm safe up here... but I’ll have to climb down at some point."
^And so, he studied the enemy’s swings for hours. Until he felt ready. And then he climbed down—to look death in the eyes. And then—miracle of miracles—his parry connected.
^The caveman dropped like a sack of meat.
^Mial, now unburdened by mercy or patience, delivered a final slash so vicious that the caveman’s ancestors felt it. He had discovered the ancient and noble art of parrying.
^"I took no damage," he whispered, eyes wide. "This is power. This is divinity."
^Drunk on success and borderline delusional, Mial considered casting off his armor altogether. Who needed it? He had reflexes now. He had timing. He had... hubris.
^Outside the cave, he swaggered up to a bandit and attempted another parry—cold, confident, and catastrophically wrong.
^The bandit didn’t swing. The bandit stabbed. Mial, shocked and armorless, exploded in a glorious display of overconfidence.

^The moral, stained in blood and irony: never parry what you haven’t studied. Let them swing first. Let them fail. Dodge until you’ve learned their rhythm—or climb a rock and wait. Only then, maybe, should you raise your arms and parry away.
^Also, wear armor. Especially pants. And if you’re riding a horse—put on the damn helmet.
